articles.title: Criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate in Alaska
articles.summary: By Andrew Goudsward and Nathan Frandino WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, US officials said on Friday, injecting fresh uncertainty into Tuesday's congressional midterm election. The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, ‌said at a press conference that a Wednesday New York Times article about the effort had driven a "surge" of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the ‌case and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly." "Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," he said. "Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they'll answer for it." Separately, the department on Friday ​asked a federal judge to block Alaska from certifying the election results if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, also named Daniel Sullivan. The contest between Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is widely seen as one of the few Senate races that could sway control of the chamber on November 3. A record 48 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail. If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations into Trump's ‌administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against ⁠Iran. KEY PATH FOR DEMOCRATS If Democrats cannot flip the seat, their path to a majority narrows considerably, with the party needing to win at least two other races in mostly Republican states such as Ohio, Texas, Iowa and Kansas. Trump's fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the US House of Representatives, ⁠according to nonpartisan analysts. The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party's Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot. Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times' reporting. Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has ​also ​denied involvement. Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign. It is not clear what, if any, laws ​may have been broken; both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known ‌candidates to siphon votes from their opponents. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted. Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the investigation proceed. He also said the probe had been ongoing for months and that the Times report had added urgency to the investigation, but did not explain how. Peltola's campaign has asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department's lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis. CALIFORNIA PROBE The Justice Department has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by noncitizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters. A US appeals court on Friday rejected the department's request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the ‌Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week. A lower court judge had ​already denied the administration's request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters. California officials have said the Justice ​Department's assertions relied on suspect data. The administration's legal moves represent an extraordinary federal intervention in ​state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington. Trump has ‌long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that ​his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was ​the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found. The president will campaign on Friday in Florida, the latest in a series of rallies he has headlined in states he won handily in 2024 but where Democrats are now competitive, as he tries to stave off Republican losses on Tuesday. Trump said on Friday he would attend weekend ​rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a day after canceling them, ‌telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 ​election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday. (Additional reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Nathan Layne, Jana Winter, Max Schwarz, Kia Johnson, Maria Tsvetkova, Doina Chiacu and Jan Wolfe; Writing ​by Joseph Ax and Jonathan Allen; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Scott Malone, Alistair Bell and Rosalba O'Brien) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-escalates-legal-challenges-against-101126175.html

articles.title: Stocks plunge on the final trading day of October as AI reckoning grips Wall Street
articles.summary: US stocks plunged in the final trading day of the month as earnings from Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) this week rekindled concerns about the amount of money Big Tech is spending on its AI ambitions. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 2.8% as a tech-fueled sell-off intensified. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.2%, or over 650 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 2%. For the month, the Dow gained 1.5%, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 gave up gains, falling 5.2% and 1.2%, respectively. October marked the worst month for the Nasdaq since March 2025. Stocks fell for the second day in a row after Amazon and Alphabet posted rare earnings misses , renewing concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amazon shares fell 2%, while Alphabet continued to erase market value after its stock suffered its worst day in over 20 years. Intel ( INTC ) also suffered a brutal reaction to its earnings report, dropping 29% in premarket trading after the company's Q4 outlook came up short. One bright spot in the market was ExxonMobil ( XOM ) and Chevron ( CVX ), whose stocks briefly touched record highs after the oil majors reported that their earnings were boosted as refining margins widened amid the war in the Middle East. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca ( AZN ) also reported an earnings beat before the opening bell. While earnings remain in focus, oil prices rebounded higher, putting additional pressure on markets. Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ) rose to $112 per barrel, while WTI crude ( CL=F ) reached $104 per barrel. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) prices tumbled more than 2% as crypto assets were rattled following a $6.3 billion hack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, marking the largest heist of its kind in history. articles.title: Judge opens probe into potential DOJ misconduct over Trump's golf course plans
articles.summary: A federal judge has opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links. Friday’s hearing became the latest fiery courtroom clash between U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes and the Department of Justice (DOJ), which repeatedly took issue with the judge’s lines of questioning and pushed back on any suggestion that information was wrongly withheld. “The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and DOJ attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules,” the judge said. A preservationist group and local golfers are suing to stop major redevelopments at East Potomac Park, the longtime home of a public golf course along the edge of the nation’s capital. Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire to redevelop it into a championship-style course, and in recent days, he has said the site will close beginning Nov. 15 so the project can proceed. The president’s comments — and recent work to cut down hundreds of trees — have escalated the legal fight. In a flurry of recent hearings in Reyes’s courtroom, the judge whom former President Biden appointed has repeatedly torn into DOJ attorneys about their representations on the status of the project, suggesting they were telling her something different and not to believe the president. Reyes began on Friday by reminding the DOJ’s No. 3 official, Stanley Woodward, about professional ethics rules he is bound to follow as an attorney practicing before the court. As they continued to spar, the judge at one point told Woodward to “finish that thought internally” and to “talk about it at drinks with your friends.” “We’re not on TV. I’m not a pundit,” Woodward pushed back at another point, also suggesting some of the judge’s questioning was blocked under executive privilege. The judge announced she was opening the investigation after learning that the government has been working to submit the redesign plan to the National Capital Planning Commission, which examines major government projects in the Washington area. Reyes expressed frustration that the DOJ hadn’t previously told her about it. She said she’ll conduct the investigation herself or appoint a special master to do so. As of now, the judge has restricted further tree-clearing at the golf course and has implemented new notice requirements, but she hasn’t yet outright blocked the planned closure. “Trust but verify … no longer,” Reyes warned the government. articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed leads Michigan Senate polls, but a divide among Dems could hurt him
articles.summary: On Election Day, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers will face off in what may be the marquee battle of the 2026 midterms: the race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters in Michigan. It's a contest that could decide which party controls the U.S. Senate. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who caucus with them. They need 51 to win back the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.) Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible , but Democrats are also playing defense in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan. The Great Lakes State looks like the closest of the three. Democrats are pinning their hopes on El-Sayed , an unapologetic 41-year-old progressive who's pushing policies such as Medicare for All and ending U.S. military aid to Israel; who's willing to confront his critics and his own party's establishment; and who's vying to become America's first Muslim senator. Republicans have handed the reins to Rogers , a 63-year-old former congressman who lost an extremely close Senate race to Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, and who has since broken with President Trump on tariffs and the war in Iran. The race has been rocked by several controversies, including the revelation this week that the fiancé of Rep. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the primary, will not join her in voting for El-Sayed due to his frequent criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza. "Every time [El-Sayed] talks about genocide, Jews get death threats," Stevens's fiancé, a Michigan lawyer and registered Democrat named Jason Turkish, claimed Wednesday at a Rogers campaign event . "We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul." The Associated Press reported Thursday that Stevens — who has urged El-Sayed to reach out to her supporters — will campaign with him this weekend. It'll be their first time appearing together since August. Further raising the stakes is the fact that Michigan couldn't be more purple, having swung to Trump in 2016, then Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, then back to Trump in 2024 — always by slim margins. Here's everything you need to know about the Michigan Senate contest. Who's winning? Here's what the polls say. Twelve polls have been conducted in October. Eleven of them have shown El-Sayed with leads ranging from 1 to 7 percentage points . New surveys from both CBS Detroit and CNN give El-Sayed a 7-point lead. The only recent poll to show Rogers ahead (by 2 points) was sponsored by a group affiliated with the former congressman . To close the gap on Election Day, Rogers has been reaching out to two groups who backed Stevens over El-Sayed in the primary: Black and Jewish Democrats. In August, Stevens won a majority of Michigan's large counties with significant Black populations by an average of 8.5 percentage points . She also won Detroit with more than 60% of the vote, making El-Sayed the first Michigan Democrat since 2018 to win a statewide primary without winning the state's largest city. El-Sayed shakes hands with former President Barack Obama during a campaign event on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some members of Michigan's Jewish community also gravitated toward Stevens because El-Sayed has called the war in Gaza a "genocide" and accused Democrats who refuse to do the same of lacking the courage necessary "to stand up to Donald Trump." "Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil," El-Sayed told CNN in April . "It's not how evil is this one versus that one. Hamas: evil. Israeli government: evil. We can say both." It remains to be seen whether Rogers's outreach will pay off; he's also targeting more reliable Republican constituencies such as the nearly 4 million Michiganders ages 50 and older. So far, polls suggest that El-Sayed's strategy — trying to maximize his support among anti-establishment voters, Arab Americans and young voters — has put him ahead in the polls. But the polls have overestimated El-Sayed before. In the run-up to August's primary, several surveys showed El-Sayed with a double-digit lead over Stevens. The race ended up being much closer than expected, with El-Sayed edging Stevens by less than 1 percentage point . How controversial has the race been? El-Sayed's background has also made him the target of persistent attacks from Republicans, with Trump going so far as to call him a "jihadist" and accuse him of being "on the side of the terrorists." Vice President JD Vance recently said El-Sayed had "zero attachment" to the United States. El-Sayed is a U.S. citizen who was born and raised in Michigan. Rogers has claimed without evidence that El-Sayed has supported the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups. In a recent exchange at a town hall with a critic who asked him whether he denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, El-Sayed highlighted what he called the "implicit" suggestion in the question: the assumption that he'll have "dual loyalties" because of his faith. "I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim." After Trump referred to El-Sayed as " Mohammed " — his middle name — the Democrat responded in what has become his signature pugnacious style. "I don't care how he pronounces my name," El-Sayed said during a rally in Grand Rapids on Sunday. "Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." Trump watches a video of El-Sayed during a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Mich. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Meanwhile, El-Sayed has campaigned with Hasan Piker , a Marxist streamer whom other Democrats have called antisemitic and even anti-American . "If perfectly inoffensive won elections, then Donald Trump would never have been president," El-Sayed said in April when reporters questioned his choice of allies. An independent left-wing group affiliated with Piker's uncle, commentator Cenk Uygur, also recently released an ad linking U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices. The ad shows two parents shopping for their kids' lunch items; the mom tells the dad to put a carton of eggs back on the shelf. "They don't like eggs anymore?" the dad asks. "No, they like eggs," the mom answers. "But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians." Some Democrats and Republicans have urged El-Sayed to denounce the content of the ad rather than just distancing himself from it. "That has nothing to do with our campaign," El-Sayed said of the ad. "It's certainly not what I want to be talking about right now." Who is El-Sayed? El-Sayed, 41, was born on Halloween 1984 in Rochester Hills, Mich. — a northern suburb of Detroit. His parents were immigrants from Egypt, and his first language was Arabic. He captained his high school's wrestling, football and lacrosse teams, then continued to play club lacrosse at the University of Michigan, where he majored in biology and political science. El-Sayed went on to study medicine at Michigan, Oxford University (as a Rhodes Scholar) and Columbia University, where he received his MD. Before politics, he pursued a career in public health epidemiology as a tenure-track professor, and later led the Detroit health department. In 2017, El-Sayed, then just 32, resigned as Detroit's health director to run for governor. He said at the time he was inspired by his work on the Flint water crisis . He was endorsed by prominent progressives — Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer by more than 20 percentage points. After a stint as Wayne County health director, El-Sayed decided to try again in 2026. He has since become the most prominent Democratic insurgent to channel left-wing disillusionment with politics and outrage over Israel's actions in Gaza to win his party's nomination in a state where more moderate candidates typically prevail. His argument is that even in so-called purple states such as Michigan, Democrats have a better shot at success when they pick buzzy, big-swing progressives over safe, "electable" incrementalists. Who is Rogers? Rogers was born in Livingston County, Mich., in 1963. He earned a bachelor's degree in criminal justice and sociology from Adrian College in 1985 before joining the Army. After four years of military service, Rogers joined the FBI as a special agent based in Chicago. His work with federal law enforcement focused on countering organized crime and public corruption. Rogers began his political career in 1994, when he was elected to a seat in the Michigan state legislature. He served for six years before launching his first bid for Congress. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina campaigns for Rogers in Muskegon, Mich., on Oct. 30, 2026. AP Photo/Paul Sancya Rogers was elected to the House of Representatives in one of the closest races of the 2000 election cycle, defeating Democrat Dianne Byrum by just 111 votes . During his 14-year tenure in the House, Rogers was a key conservative voice on national security and intelligence issues. He spent four years as chairman of the powerful House Intelligence Committee, much of that time focused on what he describes as "the economic and national security danger posed by China." Rogers left Congress in 2015 and quickly began a career in media. He hosted a daily syndicated radio show called Something to Think About with Mike Rogers and worked as a commentator for CNN. Rogers returned to run for the Senate in 2024. Roughly six months after that loss, he announced his plan to run again in 2026. Rogers is a conservative Republican on most issues — including abortion, immigration and transgender rights — but his opinion on Trump has shifted through the years. Over the past few weeks, Rogers has retreated from his early support for the president on two key issues: calling for Trump to end the "tariff war" with Canada and saying the conflict in Iran should also "end quickly." articles.title: Student-loan relief delays are trapping public service workers in debt, lawsuit says
articles.summary: A new lawsuit against the Trump administration targets delays in processing Public Service Loan Forgiveness for thousands of student-loan borrowers. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images The Education Department is facing a new lawsuit over the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. The lawsuit said the department is failing to process buyback applications and is illegally rescinding borrowers' payments. These delays are forcing borrowers to pay off loans that should be forgiven, the lawsuit said. The Trump administration is facing another lawsuit over claims it's mishandling student-loan forgiveness for thousands of borrowers. On Friday, the American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten filed a lawsuit against the Department of Education over stalled debt relief for borrowers pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness , which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years. The lawsuit, which is seeking class-action status, said that the department has failed to process the buyback applications of 90,000 borrowers, which allows borrowers to "buy back" months spent in deferment or forbearance if those months would put them at the threshold for relief. The lawsuit also said the department has illegally rescinded payments borrowers have made toward the program, "trapping in debt borrowers whose loans should be forgiven." It includes Donald Knierim, who previously spoke to Business Insider , as a declarant in the case. Knierim retired after being notified that he had achieved PSLF, only to have 15 of his payments rescinded months later. Advocacy group Protect Borrowers is representing the AFT. Its senior counsel, Laura Dismore, said in a statement that PSLF borrowers "deserve better than more dysfunction and broken promises." "The law guarantees public service workers certain rights, and we will enforce those rights wherever and whenever they are violated," Dismore said. The Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Ongoing Public Service Loan Forgiveness challenges Business Insider has heard from public service workers over the past who have faced a slew of challenges with PSLF. For example, the PSLF payment tracker has not updated for many borrowers, leaving those who made their final payments waiting for their relief to be processed. The continued backlog of buyback processing has been an added strain; the department's most recent status report in a separate lawsuit filed by the AFT said that 88,000 applications were pending. The department said some borrowers submitted multiple buyback requests, which inflated the backlog. More recently, PSLF borrowers like Knierim received notices that the payments they had made toward forgiveness no longer count, extending some borrowers' repayment timelines by years. The department said the clawbacks were due to Biden-era coding errors. All of the listed delays to relief are actively harming borrowers in public service, the lawsuit said. For example, Elizabeth Schoepflin, one of the plaintiffs, said that the Education Department "ripped away the loan forgiveness credit I earned without any explanation." "Every month this drags on is another payment I shouldn't have to make," she said. David Petley, another plaintiff, said he's been waiting over a year and a half for his buyback application to be approved. "I am expected to keep making more expensive monthly payments in the meantime," he said. These challenges come as the Trump administration is implementing its student-loan repayment overhaul , which includes new repayment plans and borrowing caps. While borrowers have reported surging monthly bills under the plan, the administration has said its changes are intended to simplify a complex repayment system and curb excessive borrowing. Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com . If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo. articles.title: 'I'm deeply hurt': Christa Pike speaks after surviving lethal injection
articles.summary: Christa Pike is speaking out publicly for the first time since she survived an execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said in her first public statement since the execution attempt, which her legal team shared Friday. "My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul." Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, and spent 30 years on death row. Two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her during the state's execution attempt last month. She was taken to the hospital, where she received lifesaving care. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez , described the situation as a "mess" and said she was left without justice. “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said. "I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured." Pike's legal team described the outcome as "unprecedented" and said it has raised questions about what happens next in her case. "I don't know why I survived that night," Pike added. "I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone." Pike's survival has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year, and the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, is stepping down at the end of October. Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. They said the botched execution "reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement issued earlier this month, according to ABC News . Pike has been held at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center since Oct. 10, where she has been behind bars for more than 30 years. She continues to receive medical care in the prison's infirmary. "I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," her statement read. "But healing is not the same as being okay." What was Christa Pike's condition after the botched execution? When Pike arrived at the hospital, her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers wrote in a legal filing on Oct. 2. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream. Her condition was so severe in the following days, after the execution attempt, that it was believed that she may be brain-dead and could be removed from life support the following day, Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said during a press conference on Oct. 7. "On Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking," he said. Spivey added that Pike is feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital and is still dealing with major physical problems from the failed execution, including a blood clot, pneumonia and swelling that has left her unable to use both of her arms. "Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team wrote in a court filing on Oct. 6. Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health will not be clear for some time. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here." Pike, pictured in 2007, is conscious and speaking in the hospital, according to her legal team. via REUTERS / REUTERS Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, told the BBC that she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking. "They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," she said. "This has never happened before." Dr. Zivot told the BBC that her survival was "unusual," adding, "Most people who get lethal injection die from it. In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa." Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo told the Associated Press, "There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through." The incident with Pike comes a handful of months after the botched attempt to execute Tony Carruthers . In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm, but were unable to insert a secondary IV line. What happens next? All executions in Tennessee are paused for now. Pike's lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted. State officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, and Gov. Lee has not indicated that he plans to intervene in Pike's case. Lee had denied Pike's clemency before the execution attempt. "I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell told CNN's State of the Union earlier this month. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her." Dr. Zivot said it remains unclear how much pentobarbital entered Pike's system, how much remained in her blood after the injection and what effects she could still experience as she recovers. "I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said. Professor Russo doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double jeopardy grounds — the constitutional protection against being tried or punished twice for the same offense — should it decide to do so. He said, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution." "We're in uncharted territory," Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told USA Today . "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947. These are questions that have never needed to be asked before, and no one knows the answers." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/christa-pike-speaks-out-in-1st-public-statement-after-failed-execution-i-dont-know-why-i-survived-144956746.html
articles.author: Tom Parfitt, Mike Bebernes, Kate Murphy

articles.title: Netanyahu's party claims election was stolen as results show him losing majority
articles.summary: Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset. Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government. The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53. Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population. "Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran." The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect. The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power. Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister. "No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise" The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear. "An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement. The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections." Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters. Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation. "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians." "An improper influence operation?" While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins. Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results. "Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post. Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on —   Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament. Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically , will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/israel-election-results-netanyahu-likud-claim-stolen-arab-parties/
articles.author: Dov Lieber

articles.title: 'It could be quite a brutal evening': GOP braces for some once-unthinkable losses
articles.summary: Republicans are bracing for a brutal election night, convinced they're set to face some previously unthinkable losses in deep-red Trump territory as key battleground races hang on a knife's edge . House Republicans are privately discussing not just if they'll lose their majority, but by how many seats. Imperiled GOP incumbents in once safe districts have been begging party leaders for more money in the final few days to stem the bleeding, according to six people involved in internal conversations, granted anonymity to discuss them. Senate Republicans have found new cause to worry about contests in Ohio, Kansas and other red states. "It could be quite a brutal evening," said one senior Republican involved in the private conversations, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Once the dominoes start falling it becomes hard to stop them." Some Republican incumbents made an eyebrow-raising emergency decision. They stopped doing their own polling weeks ago as they tried to save every dollar for swaying voters as they begged for the GOP cavalry to arrive from President Donald Trump's political operation to the National Republican Congressional Committee, according to three of the people. One Republican strategist working on midterm races simply responded to a question about the environment with a video of a dumpster on fire that was being swept away by flood waters. Top GOP officials and lawmakers have long known the political landscape would be bad, amid voter anger over the cost of living and aspects of Trump's policy agenda. But they're facing a worse position than they expected earlier this year, with less than one week until Election Day. Republicans for weeks have worried that young men who'd voted for Trump, including white and Hispanic working class voters, will stay home amid disillusionment with high costs and the Iran war. That alone could allow Democrats to overperform in some areas after they hemorrhaged support among that voting bloc in 2024. At a Kwik Trip in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, this week in the hotly-contested 3rd District, Isaiah Romero was filling up his silver Ram truck. The 20-year-old said he cast his ballot for Trump in his first ever presidential election two years ago. His verdict on high fuel prices? "I think they're bull," he said as he looked over to the $6.39 per gallon diesel and $4.29 gas at the pump. Is he voting this time? "No," Romero responded, adding: "I didn't vote for this." New fires have been popping up across the map just as soon as top GOP officials put out others. Trump canceled in-person rallies in deep-red Kansas and Iowa set for this weekend to instead hold a series of tele-rallies for GOP candidates in the final stretch. "Any Democrats telling you they aren't winning the Senate [besides] a couple of seats are sandbagging expectations," the senior Republican said. In Ohio, the race between GOP Sen. Jon Husted and former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is still incredibly close in private and public polling. But Republicans have watched with horror as GOP governor nominee "Vivek's [Ramaswamy's] numbers have gone off a cliff" in the last few days after he ran an ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother saying her daughter is a liar, according to the senior Republican and two others who saw the internal polling. Acton's stepfather was charged with raping her when she was 12. The headwinds across all of Ohio are deeply problematic for Republicans. They now believe embattled Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) — who is facing child and domestic abuse allegations that he denies — will lose in a seat Trump won by double digits. South Carolina has become another unexpectedly nailbiting race for Republicans, where political newcomer Sen. Darline Graham is facing a well-funded Democratic challenger. But GOP operatives and officials are feeling somewhat better after outside groups injected cash into the race earlier this month and Trump announced another rally in the state to energize Republicans' base. "It's a lot closer than I think we would ever want, but I think she's going to pull it out," said Jeff Davis, chair of the Greenville County Republican Party. But in one of the most dire signs, once-unimaginable GOP worries have started to creep about deep-red Louisiana — where Trump announced this week he will hold an election-eve tele-rally for Senate nominee Julia Letlow. Speaker Mike Johnson, who is close with Letlow, will join as Republicans have grown wary about a surge of Black voters and other Democratic-leaning voters in early voting across the South. Senior Republicans believe Letlow will win, but they fear it will be by single digits if nothing changes. "The cakewalk turned into a knife fight," said one Louisiana Republican who has talked with Letlow recently. "If Democrat turnout surges on Election Day, it'll be a long night in Monroe," the person added, and they expect Letlow to win by just 6 points in a state Trump won by 22 points two years ago. In another painful development for Republicans in Louisiana, GOP groups have even started an eye-popping spending war in a safe red gerrymandered seat — where a bitter Republican-on-Republican primary is unfolding between state Sen. Blake Miguez, who was formerly endorsed by Trump , and state Sen. Rick Edmonds, Johnson's former pastor. Club for Growth poured another $220,000 into the race Thursday. Republicans fear the messy race is poised for a December runoff. "POLITICO's sad little rolodex of loser strategists have no idea what they're talking about, and if they really believe what they're saying they should come out of the shadows and put a name to their brain-dead comments," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. "While Republicans have focused on real solutions to improve costs of living and make our nation safer, Democrats have nominated a gang of radicals who want to raise taxes, force everyone on government healthcare, and release criminals onto the streets," said Joanna Rodriguez, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. On the House side, Republicans are bracing for a brutal night. But they've long been spending in some redder GOP districts to forestall a true disaster. Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, said that the committee worked in partnership with the campaigns and the RNC to launch coordinated advertising early in GOP-held districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (Colo.), Bill Huizenga (Mich.), Rob Wittman (Va.), Mike Turner (Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (Texas). The NRCC began airing coordinated ads in early August, more than a month before the DCCC. The NRCC also conducted polling in more than 100 districts, an eye-popping number, as they worked to see how far the fires had spread into red terrain and make sure they were moving resources where they were needed. Republicans still think they can unseat Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), while flipping retiring Rep. Jared Golden's (D-Maine) seat. But privately, Republicans believe North Carolina's open 11th District is close to gone, as are several other deep-red seats Trump won by double digits, according to four people with knowledge of the situation. And they're still not confident they'll beat Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) in a seat the GOP thought would be an easy flip when they redrew it early this year. It's become the most expensive House race in history. The Republican in Kentucky's 6th district, where Trump won by 15 points in 2024, is barely hanging on, according to the four people. Even in the South Texas districts the GOP redrew in their favor, Republicans reached the point days ago where no amount of new money is going to change the upcoming catastrophe, said one Republican official involved in conversations about those races. Johnson traveled to Minnesota on Thursday to headline a fundraiser for GOP Rep. Brad Finstad, who Republicans are scrambling to shore up in a +12 Trump district. Finstad told POLITICO in an interview this week that he had warned senior Republicans for weeks about Democratic groups pouring money into the race in his southern Minnesota district. "We raised that with anybody and everybody that would want to hear it," Finstad said. "From a global perspective, people were like, 'Well, you won by 18, you're fine.' And, you know, those of us in Minnesota know that this district has always had kind of an independent streak to it." Senate Democrats, meanwhile, are upbeat at their prospects, but public and private polling across close to the entire battleground map is running within the margin of error — meaning those states could break either way. "I would rather be us than them. But if anyone tells you they know what's going to happen, they're full of shit," one senior Senate Democratic operative said. "Everything is close." And some Republicans are taking solace in the fact that at least it'll all soon be over. "I can see the light at the end of the tunnel," said a GOP strategist working on a campaign that is trending toward Democrats. "It might be a semi-truck, but at least I can see it." Andrew Howard, Erin Doherty and Alec Hernández contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/could-quite-brutal-evening-gop-090000456.html
articles.author: Meredith Lee Hill

articles.title: U.S. scraps G20 group photo after European diplomats refuse to pose with Russia's Lavrov
articles.summary: ATLANTA (AP) — Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies appeared far apart on critical global security issues as they began meeting Friday in Atlanta, after European objections to Russia’s participation forced the U.S. hosts to cancel the traditional group photo. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such gatherings. But he still opened the talks with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. “We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.” He pointed to disruptions to global energy and food supplies , trade and freedom of navigation and said many are posing “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order.” Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran , U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea . All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade. No joint statement expected from the diplomats' meeting Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding — as is its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20. Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration's not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will likely prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up Saturday, participants said. That did not surprise Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who was representing his country in its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting. “We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters. Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's G20 leaders summit hosted by President Donald Trump in Florida a success. Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils Europeans Already poor prospects for the talks worsened when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance. However, the State Department announced Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine. Lavrov, when asked about the planned three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. next month, told Russian reporters that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s position regarding long-range strikes against Russia “doesn’t help preparation for the talks.” Moscow will not allow a situation in which Ukraine poses a “military threat to legitimate security interests of the Russian Federation,” he said. Lavrov also said Russia sees no point in inviting Poland to join the G20 meeting, adding that it “violates the principles of diplomacy” and the country “adds nothing” to the grouping. Sikorski, whose country is a strong ally of neighboring Ukraine, earlier said, “I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.” British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband explicitly called out Lavrov, saying that “if we are serious about our values and our interests we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine.” “An assault not only on Ukraine but on us all — trampling international law, sovereignty and self determination — core principles on which we all depend,” he said. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said “there is no normality with Russia” but “we must exchange the controversies at the table here,” the German news agency dpa reported. He added that “we also must not send falsely optimistic signals.” Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow, and it is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump’s invitation to attend the G20 leaders summit at his Miami golf club in December. G20 member South Africa was not invited Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland is seeking formal membership with U.S. support. But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. “We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate “on an equal footing with other members” when Britain takes over the presidency next year. The Iran war hangs over the G20 event The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz , the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors. But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. Rubio met on the sidelines with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, as well as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, whose country has been a key mediator. The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them. ___ Associated Press writers Michelle Gumede in Johannesburg, South Africa, Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jill Lawless in London and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/g20-diplomats-including-china-russia-040255027.html
